summary: Describes a standardized way to convey trunk group parameters in sip and tel URIs. It defines an extension to the tel URI for this purpose. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Phone companies group phone lines into big bundles. This note adds a way to name the bundle inside a phone address.

subtitle: A standard way to name the group of phone circuits a call used, right inside tel and sip URIs.

tldr.problem: Voice-over-IP proxies and PSTN gateways had no standard way to say which trunk group a call arrived on or should leave on, so vendors invented ad hoc names and placed them in different spots.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4904 adds two tel URI parameters, tgrp and trunk-context, which together identify a trunk group. The egress group goes in the Request-URI and the ingress group goes in the Contact header.
tldr.outcome: Proxies and gateways from different vendors can agree on where trunk groups appear and what they mean, as long as the nodes trust each other.

today: RFC 4904 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. The text says the new tel URI parameters are registered through the separate tel URI parameter registry document rather than by this RFC.

sections.title: Trunks, Trunk Groups and the Problem
sections.content:
In the telephone network (the PSTN), calls are routed over circuits called trunks between switches. A trunk group is a set of interchangeable trunks that are traffic engineered as a unit. Trunk groups have labels, and switches use those labels to know which switch came before and which comes next.

A SIP to PSTN gateway may have trunks connected to different carriers. The phone number alone does not say which carrier to use, so a trunk group can narrow the choice at the gateway. The RFC treats how a proxy picks a trunk group as out of scope. It only standardizes how to write the choice in signaling messages.

The problem statement names two ambiguities. Positional ambiguity: a proxy might put the trunk group in the user part of the Request-URI or as a parameter of the Request-URI itself. Semantic ambiguity: with no standard grammar, people pick ad hoc names and values. Without a standard, a proxy from one vendor may not interoperate with a gateway from another.
sections.eli5: A phone company has bundles of lines going to different places. Nobody agreed on how to write down which bundle a call used, so each company did it differently. This note picks one way.

sections.title: Design Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC lists four requirements that shaped the design.

  • REQ 1: trunk group parameters must be defined as an extension to the tel URI. Trunk groups are tied to the PSTN, the tel URI can be reused by non-SIP VoIP protocols, and the procedures in RFC 3261 can derive an equivalent sip URI from a tel URI.
  • REQ 2: name collisions between domains must be prevented, so the trunk group needs a namespace. The existing phone-context parameter does not fit, because it applies only to local numbers and trunk groups may appear in local or global numbers.
  • REQ 3: originating and destination trunk groups must be able to appear separately and at the same time in a SIP message.
  • REQ 4: proxies and redirect servers should be able to add the destination trunk group as a route is selected.
sections.eli5: The rules were: write it in the phone-number address, give it a company label so two companies do not mix up names, allow both a "came in from" and a "going out on" label, and let the middle machines add the "going out on" one.

sections.title: The tgrp and trunk-context Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC extends the par rule of the tel URI (RFC 3966) with two new parameters: ;tgrp= followed by a trunk group label, and ;trunk-context= followed by a descriptor. The label is one or more unreserved or escaped characters, plus the extra characters /, &, + and $.

Both parameters MUST be present to identify a trunk group, and implementations MUST generate both. If a receiver sees only one of them, it MUST act as if there were no trunk group parameters at all.

The trunk-context sets the scope of the label. It can hold four kinds of value: a specific host (a gateway), a subdomain such as north.example.com covering some gateways in a domain, a provider domain such as example.com covering all its gateways, or a global number or its leading digits for provider-wide scoping. Unlike phone-context, it may appear in local or global tel URIs.

Two URIs with trunk group parameters are compared with the normal base comparison rules for tel and sip URIs.
sections.eli5: A trunk group is written with two labels: the name of the bundle and the company or building whose naming list it belongs to. You need both, like a first name and a family name. With only one, you pretend you saw neither.

sections.title: Where Each Party Puts and Reads Trunk Groups
sections.content:
The terminating (egress) trunk group MUST be in the Request-URI. It tells the next downstream entity which trunk group to use, and it lets a proxy add it as it picks a route. The originating (ingress) trunk group MUST be in the Contact header URI, which is a sip or sips URI. The RFC argues against putting it in the From URI, because a From URI names a resource long term while a trunk group binding lasts only for the session.

Because of the normal Contact rules in RFC 3261, later requests in the dialog, such as a BYE, carry that Contact URI as their Request-URI. The gateway can then tie the call back to the right trunk group and free resources.

  • User agent client: MUST include the originating trunk group in the Contact. It MAY insert the destination trunk group if it knows the topology.
  • User agent server (gateway): a trunk group in the Request-URI means use that group. If all circuits are busy it MAY send a 603 Decline. If it is not configured with the group, it SHOULD NOT use another one, and it MAY reject with 404. If it is not authoritative for the trunk-context, it MUST ignore the tgrp value.
  • Proxy: SHOULD NOT change trunk group parameters in the Contact. It MAY insert destination parameters in the Request-URI if none are present, and SHOULD NOT change existing ones unless it has better knowledge of the topology.
sections.eli5: The "going out on" label goes on the address you are sending to. The "came in from" label goes on the return address, so replies know their way back. Middle machines may add the first label but should leave the second alone.

sections.title: Example Call Flows
sections.content:
The RFC's reference setup has a SIP proxy and three gateways. Calls arrive from the PSTN at GW1 on trunk group TG1-1. GW2 and GW3 are egress gateways, and the group TG2-2 is shared between them.

In the basic flow, GW1 sends an INVITE to the proxy with the ingress group in the Contact. The proxy rewrites the Request-URI to add the egress group TG2-1 and sends it to GW2. When GW2 later hangs up, its BYE uses the original Contact, trunk group included, as the Request-URI, so GW1 can match the call to its trunk group.

If a call from the PSTN has no calling party number, the gateway MUST create a tel URI with a locally generated token (for example a line or port number), because the tel scheme does not allow an empty URI.

In the inter-domain flow, a call is retargeted from example.com to example.net. The other domain does not interpret the trunk group parameters, since they are not its own, and simply echoes the Contact back as the Request-URI of later requests.

Three tel to sip conversion examples are given, such as tel:+16305550100;tgrp=TG-1;trunk-context=example.com, which becomes a sip URI with the parameters in the user part and user=phone at the end.
sections.eli5: A call comes in on line bundle TG1-1 and leaves on bundle TG2-1. When someone hangs up, the message goes back using the saved return address, so the first building knows which bundle to free up.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Trunk group parameters only modify an address, so existing trust between sender and receiver is unchanged. Still, tampering has real effects. An attacker who knows the name of a toll-free trunk could change the Request-URI to get free service or shift traffic between trunks. Changing the Contact could make a routing node tie a call to the wrong source.

The attack class and protections are the same as for baseline SIP. The SIPS scheme and TLS SHOULD be used for integrity protection. Inside a domain, a proxy should accept trunk groups from a gateway only over SIPS and should challenge with HTTP Digest, while a gateway should check the proxy's X.509 certificate. Between domains, the receiving proxy may rely on the sender's certificate identity.

Trunk group parameters are only meaningful among mutually trusting nodes. A node receiving a request from an untrusted upstream node SHOULD remove them. They can also reveal least-cost routing, peering and network topology, so a carrier may choose not to include them, and TLS SHOULD be used if confidentiality matters.
sections.eli5: Someone sneaky could change the bundle name to use a cheaper or free line. So you send the note in a sealed envelope, and you ignore bundle names from people you do not trust.

layers.label: Request-URI
layers.detail: Destination (egress) trunk group: tgrp plus trunk-context

layers.label: Contact header URI
layers.detail: Originating (ingress) trunk group: tgrp plus trunk-context

layers.label: From URI
layers.detail: Not used; it names a long-term resource, not a session binding
